name: Sunscreen-maxxing

lead: Sunscreen-maxxing means wearing sunscreen every day and reapplying it, to keep UV from building up photodamage: fewer wrinkles and dark spots, and smoother skin over the years.

Sunscreens filter or block UV radiation. SPF, introduced by Franz Greiter in 1974, mainly reflects UVB protection, and broad-spectrum labels indicate UVA protection too. A randomised Australian trial found that daily broad-spectrum use for 4.5 years was associated with smoother, more resilient skin than usual habits. Reference sources also report that sunscreen can help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma.

paras: People apply a broad-spectrum sunscreen on the face and exposed skin every morning and reapply through the day when outdoors. It is usually paired with other sun-protection habits and skincare. Studies find many people apply too little.
Reported issues include allergic contact dermatitis and, in some aerosols, benzene contamination. Typical use is not usually linked to vitamin D deficiency. Ingredient rules differ by country.

angle.text: Sunscreen-maxxing means strict daily SPF use with regular reapplication to limit UV-driven skin aging. Blocking UV means less photodamage accumulates, so fewer wrinkles and dark spots develop. A randomised Australian trial found smoother skin after 4.5 years of daily broad-spectrum use.

lead: Sunscreen-maxxing is the looksmaxxing term for strict daily sunscreen use, with regular reapplication, to limit ultraviolet exposure and the skin ageing attributed to it. Its appeal for appearance is that chronic UV exposure drives wrinkles, laxity, freckles, dark spots and visible blood vessels, so blocking UV is a way to keep skin smoother, more even and younger-looking for longer.[1][2]

Sunscreens are rated by sun protection factor (SPF), introduced by Franz Greiter in 1974, which mainly reflects protection against UVB.[1] Broad-spectrum products also protect against UVA, which penetrates deeper and damages collagen and elastin.[1][2] Wikipedia describes sunscreen as one of the best ways to slow visible ageing, and photoageing references name sun protection as the most effective primary prevention.[1][2]

A 2013 Australian trial of about 900 participants reported that daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for 4.5 years was associated with smoother, more resilient skin than usual habits, and a smaller 32-person study reported that daily SPF 30 reversed photoageing signs within 12 weeks, with the improvement lasting through a year.[1] Reference sources also report that sunscreen can help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma.[1]
infobox: Sunscreen (OTC drug in the US; cosmetic in the EU)[1]

paras: Practitioners apply sunscreen every day, including on cloudy days or indoors near windows, and reapply during the day. Wikipedia reports that product directions usually advise reapplication about every two hours and after swimming or sweating.[1][2]

sections.h: Why sun protection matters for appearance
paras: Chronic UVA and UVB exposure drives photoageing. UVB mainly affects the epidermis and stimulates melanin production, which can cause freckles and dark spots, while UVA reaches the dermis and damages collagen and elastin, contributing to loss of firmness and wrinkling around the eyes, mouth and forehead.[2] UV also triggers enzymes that break down collagen and reduces new collagen production, and UVA can dilate or break blood vessels, most visibly on the nose and cheeks.[2]

Photoageing references list topical retinoids such as tretinoin, antioxidants such as vitamin C, peels, lasers, fillers and botulinum toxin among treatments, and name sun protection as the key preventive measure.[2]

SPF expresses the fraction of burn-causing UV that reaches the skin under standardised application of 2 mg per square centimetre; SPF 15 allows roughly one-fifteenth through.[1] A higher SPF does not last longer on the skin, so reapplication is still advised.[1] For the face, about a quarter to a third of a teaspoon corresponds to the tested amount, and studies have found many people apply a quarter to a half of it, reducing effective protection.[1]

Broad-spectrum labels denote UVA protection proportional to UVB protection under 2012 US FDA rules; the EU requires a UVA protection factor of at least one-third of the SPF.[1] Mineral filters (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) can leave a white cast that consumers often dislike, while chemical filters absorb UV and release it as heat.[1]

A 2013 trial in Australia, summarised on Wikipedia, followed about 900 participants; those assigned to daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for 4.5 years showed smoother, more resilient skin than those continuing usual use.[1] A smaller 32-person study reported that daily SPF 30 use reversed photoageing signs within 12 weeks, with the improvement lasting through a year.[1]

Reported adverse effects include allergic contact dermatitis, with oxybenzone and cinnamates listed as sensitisers.[1] Moderate sunscreen use can reduce vitamin D synthesis, though diet and supplements can cover it.[1] Independent testing found benzene contamination in 27 percent of aerosol sunscreens tested, leading to voluntary recalls.[1] The US banned PABA and trolamine salicylate as ingredients in 2021.[1]

In the US sunscreen is regulated as an over-the-counter drug; in the EU it is a cosmetic with labels capped at SPF 50+.[1] Hawaii banned oxybenzone and octinoxate in 2018 and Palau banned several filters in 2020, citing coral reefs.[1]

timeline.event: H. A. Milton Blake formulates what is described as the first sunscreen (10% tannic acid).[1]
US FDA rules define broad-spectrum labelling.[1]
